prompt: Two load balancers share a VIP using their distinct physical MACs, without a shared virtual MAC. After failover, local clients can establish new connections, but external clients cannot. A capture shows the upstream router still sending VIP traffic to the failed node's MAC. Which explanation fits?

options.text: DNS still points at the old load balancer's IP
options.explanation: The VIP itself hasn't changed; only which machine owns it. DNS maps names to IPs and is unaffected by which MAC answers for that IP.

options.text: The router's ARP cache still maps the VIP to the failed machine's MAC, because it ignored or never received the gratuitous ARP
options.explanation: Correct. The capture establishes a stale IP-to-MAC mapping. An announcement may have been lost, filtered or rejected. How long it persists depends on neighbour handling and configuration.

options.text: The router needs a new route to the VIP
options.explanation: The VIP is on the same subnet as before, so the router's route is unchanged. What's wrong is the link-layer delivery on the final hop.

options.text: TCP connections can't survive failover, so clients must reconnect
options.explanation: Existing connection survival depends on replicated state. Failure of new connections plus frames addressed to the old MAC identifies a link-layer delivery problem.

workedExample: The VIP is unchanged, but its active physical MAC has changed. Local clients learned the new mapping; the capture shows the router has not. Check announcement delivery, neighbour-update policy and any static mapping. A shared virtual MAC avoids changing this ARP mapping, but then switches must learn the virtual MAC's new port. Neither design guarantees an immediate recovery time.
